# On the Total Disconnectedness of the Quotient Aubry Set

This paper investigates the fine structure of the quotient Aubry set associated with a broad class of Lagrangians, establishing as its central result that this set is totally disconnected. In topological terms, total disconnectedness means that every connected component of the quotient Aubry set reduces to a single point. This is a strong structural constraint, as it precludes the existence of nontrivial continua within the set and thereby imposes a rigid geometric organization on the underlying dynamical objects.

The total disconnectedness property occupies a prominent place in the theory, and the authors present it as the principal contribution of their work. Within the framework of weak KAM theory and Aubry-Mather theory, the quotient Aubry set arises naturally as the metric space obtained by collapsing the Aubry set according to the Mañé distance. Understanding its topological structure is therefore essential for a deeper comprehension of the global dynamics governed by the associated Lagrangian and Hamiltonian systems. By demonstrating that this quotient space is totally disconnected, the paper clarifies a subtle and previously delicate aspect of its geometry.

A key theme developed throughout the paper is the intimate connection between this disconnectedness problem and a Morse-Sard type property. The Morse-Sard theorem, in its classical form, concerns the measure-theoretic size of the set of critical values of a sufficiently smooth function. In the present setting, the authors identify an analogous property that turns out to control the topological behavior of the quotient Aubry set, thereby bridging a question of geometric topology with one rooted in analysis and differential calculus.

More precisely, this Morse-Sard type property is formulated in terms of the difference of critical subsolutions of the associated Hamilton-Jacobi equations. Critical subsolutions play a fundamental role in weak KAM theory, and the differences between such subsolutions encode important information about the structure of the Aubry set. By establishing that these differences satisfy an appropriate Morse-Sard type condition, the authors are able to translate this analytic regularity into the desired conclusion of total disconnectedness. In this way, the paper not only resolves a structural question about the quotient Aubry set but also reveals a fruitful interplay between the theory of Hamilton-Jacobi equations and classical results in differential topology.

# On the Total Disconnectedness of the Quotient Aubry Set

## Introduction and Motivation

The study of Lagrangian and Hamiltonian dynamical systems has been profoundly enriched over the past decades by the development of weak KAM theory and Aubry-Mather theory. These frameworks provide powerful tools for understanding the global structure of orbits in systems that may not be integrable, and they reveal deep connections between dynamics, the calculus of variations, and the theory of viscosity solutions to Hamilton-Jacobi equations.

Central to this theory is the notion of the Aubry set, a compact invariant subset of the phase space that captures the recurrent behavior of action-minimizing trajectories. Closely related is the projected Aubry set and, most importantly for the present work, the *quotient Aubry set*. This latter object is obtained by collapsing the Aubry set according to a natural pseudmetric—the Mañé potential restricted to the Aubry set—which measures the "cost" of connecting points via calibrated curves. Two points are identified when their mutual distance in this pseudometric vanishes, and the resulting quotient space, endowed with the induced metric, encodes essential information about the number and arrangement of the elementary invariant pieces of the dynamics.

## The Central Problem

A fundamental question, raised by Mather and pursued by numerous authors, concerns the topological structure of this quotient Aubry set. In particular, one asks whether the quotient Aubry set is *totally disconnected*—that is, whether every connected component reduces to a single point. Such a property would confirm that the recurrent structure decomposes into pieces that are, in an appropriate sense, well separated, with no continuum of distinct minimizing classes.

Mather himself established total disconnectedness under certain dimensional restrictions and posed the general problem, which has since motivated considerable research. Understanding this structural feature is not merely a matter of topological curiosity: it bears directly on questions of Mañé's genericity conjectures, the finiteness of Mather classes, and the qualitative behavior of Hamiltonian flows.

## The Approach via Morse-Sard Type Properties

In this paper, the authors investigate whether the quotient Aubry set associated to a broad class of Lagrangians is totally disconnected. The key innovation lies in translating this dynamical and topological question into an analytic one concerning the regularity properties of critical subsolutions of the associated Hamilton-Jacobi equation.

The strategy rests on the observation that the pseudometric defining the quotient can be represented in terms of differences of critical subsolutions. Given two critical subsolutions of the stationary Hamilton-Jacobi equation, their difference is a Lipschitz function that is, in a strong sense, "flat" along the Aubry set. The problem of total disconnectedness can then be recast as a statement about the size of the image of such difference functions when restricted to the projected Aubry set.

This is precisely where a **Morse-Sard type property** enters. The classical Morse-Sard theorem asserts that the set of critical values of a sufficiently smooth function has Lebesgue measure zero. In the present setting, the authors establish an analogous property for the differences of critical subsolutions: the relevant set of "critical values" associated with these differences is negligible. Because the connected components of the quotient Aubry set correspond, through this analytic dictionary, to level structures of such difference functions, the smallness guaranteed by the Morse-Sard property forces each component to collapse to a point.

## Main Result

Combining these ingredients, the authors prove their central theorem:

> **The quotient Aubry set is totally disconnected.** Every connected component of the quotient Aubry set consists of a single point.

This result is obtained by carefully exploiting the regularity of critical subsolutions—drawing on the fact that critical subsolutions can be taken to be $C^{1,1}$, or approximated with sufficient smoothness—together with fine measure-theoretic estimates that yield the required Morse-Sard type conclusion for their differences. The interplay between the differentiability properties available for weak KAM solutions and the structure of the Aubry set is essential to closing the argument.

## Significance and Consequences

The total disconnectedness of the quotient Aubry set advances the understanding of the fine structure of these invariant sets within weak KAM and Aubry-Mather theory. It confirms that, despite the potential complexity of the Aubry set as a subset of phase space, its quotient by the Mañé pseudometric behaves like a "dust"—a totally disconnected space in which no nontrivial continua survive.

Beyond its intrinsic interest, this structural result has implications for the study of the number of ergodic minimizing measures, for perturbation problems in the spirit of Mañé's conjectures, and for the broader program of understanding integrability and its obstructions in Hamiltonian dynamics. By forging a bridge between the topology of the quotient Aubry set and Morse-Sard type regularity phenomena, the paper also illustrates the fruitfulness of importing analytic techniques from the theory of Hamilton-Jacobi equations into the qualitative study of Lagrangian dynamical systems.

# Aubry–Mather Theory and Lagrangian Dynamics

The study of dynamical systems has long benefited from the interplay between geometry, analysis, and the calculus of variations. Among the most influential contributions to this field is the work associated with **Aubry**, whose insights into the structure of minimizing configurations opened new avenues for understanding the long-term behavior of physical systems. Originally motivated by problems in solid-state physics—specifically the Frenkel–Kontorova model describing atoms arranged on a lattice—Aubry's ideas were later recognized as deeply connected to the theory of area-preserving maps and variational principles.

## The Role of Lagrangians

At the heart of this framework lie **Lagrangians**, the functions that encode the energy of a system in terms of positions and velocities. In classical mechanics, the dynamics of a system are determined by seeking trajectories that minimize (or more precisely, render stationary) the action integral, which is the time integral of the Lagrangian. When one considers periodic or convex Lagrangians on the torus, a rich structure of invariant sets emerges. These sets, known as Aubry and Mather sets, capture the "most stable" orbits of the system and provide a skeleton around which the more complicated dynamics organize themselves.

The beauty of the Aubry–Mather approach is that it does not require the system to be integrable. Even in the presence of chaos, one can locate special orbits that minimize the action and remain, in a well-defined sense, ordered. This makes the theory a powerful bridge between the highly regular world of integrable systems and the turbulent world of generic Hamiltonian dynamics.

## Extensions and Deeper Structure

**Moreover**, the significance of these ideas extends far beyond their original setting. The weak KAM theory developed by Fathi established a striking correspondence between the Aubry set and the solutions of the Hamilton–Jacobi equation, unifying the dynamical and the analytical perspectives. Through this lens, the Aubry set can be characterized as the region where all weak solutions of the equation coincide, giving it a canonical and intrinsic meaning.

Furthermore, these techniques have found applications in fields ranging from optimal control and homogenization to the study of geodesic flows on Riemannian manifolds. The minimizing measures introduced in this context—often called Mather measures—offer a robust tool for probing the average behavior of a system, independent of the delicate sensitivity to initial conditions that characterizes chaotic motion.

## Conclusion

In summary, the confluence of Aubry's original insights with the modern theory of Lagrangians has yielded a framework of remarkable depth and generality. It reveals that beneath the apparent complexity of many dynamical systems lies an ordered structure waiting to be uncovered. Moreover, the continued development of these ideas promises further discoveries at the intersection of geometry, physics, and analysis, reaffirming the enduring value of variational methods in mathematics.

# Abstract

We investigate the structural properties of the quotient Aubry set associated with Tonelli Hamiltonians on compact manifolds, establishing conditions under which this set is totally disconnected. The quotient Aubry set, obtained by collapsing the Aubry set via the Mañé semidistance, plays a central role in weak KAM theory and in the analysis of Hamilton-Jacobi equations, yet its topological structure remains incompletely understood in general dimensions.

Our main result demonstrates that the total disconnectedness of the quotient Aubry set is intimately linked to Morse-Sard type properties of critical subsolutions of the associated Hamilton-Jacobi equation. Specifically, we show that when critical subsolutions satisfy a suitable Sard-type condition on their sets of common calibrated points, the resulting quotient space carries no nontrivial connected components. We exploit the regularity theory of viscosity solutions, together with the differentiability properties of critical subsolutions along the Aubry set, to control the image of the projected static classes.

As a consequence, we obtain new results toward Mañé's conjecture on the generic finiteness or triviality of the quotient Aubry set. We provide explicit sufficient conditions in terms of the smoothness of the Hamiltonian and the dimension of the underlying manifold, recovering known results in low dimensions and extending them to broader settings. We further discuss counterexamples illustrating the sharpness of the Morse-Sard hypotheses and explore implications for the uniqueness of weak KAM solutions and the structure of the Mather set.

*Keywords:* Aubry-Mather theory, weak KAM theory, Hamilton-Jacobi equations, viscosity solutions, quotient Aubry set, Morse-Sard theorem, Mañé conjecture

The paper you're describing addresses a significant question in **weak KAM theory** and **Aubry-Mather theory**, connecting properties of the Aubry set to critical subsolutions of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation.

## Core Contributions

**1. Total Disconnectedness of the Quotient Aubry Set**

The main result establishes that the **quotient Aubry set** (the Aubry set equipped with the Mather/Mañé quotient pseudo-metric, then quotiented to a genuine metric space) is **totally disconnected** under appropriate hypotheses. This means its connected components are singletons—there are no non-trivial continua in the quotient space.

This is notable because it provides structural information about the Aubry set that bears on the famous **Mañé conjecture** and questions about the "smallness" of the projected Aubry set.

**2. Connection to a Morse-Sard-Type Theorem**

The key technical bridge is a **Morse-Sard theorem for differences of critical subsolutions**. The idea is:

- Critical (viscosity) subsolutions $u$ of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation $H(x, du) = c$ are Lipschitz but generally only $C^{1,1}$ near the Aubry set.
- The **difference** $u_1 - u_2$ of two critical subsolutions is **constant along the Mather quotient classes**, so it descends to a function on the quotient Aubry set.
- A Morse-Sard-type statement controls the **measure or dimension of the critical values** of these difference functions.

By showing the set of relevant critical values is small (e.g., Lebesgue-null or a set that cannot support a nontrivial connected image), one deduces that the quotient cannot contain non-degenerate connected pieces—forcing total disconnectedness.

## Significance

- **Regularity–Structure duality:** The paper exploits the interplay between the regularity of critical subsolutions (Fathi–Siconolfi and Bernard's results on $C^{1}$ and $C^{1,1}$ subsolutions) and the geometric structure of the Aubry set.
- **Dimensional constraints:** The results typically hold under **dimension hypotheses** on the underlying manifold (low-dimensional cases) or under smoothness/genericity assumptions, where the Morse-Sard machinery applies effectively.
- **Progress toward Mañé's conjecture:** Total disconnectedness of the quotient supports the broader program of understanding when the Aubry set reduces to a small, well-structured object.

# Abstract

## On the Structure of the Quotient Aubry Set and Critical Subsolutions of the Hamilton–Jacobi Equation

We investigate the fine structure of the quotient Aubry set associated with a Tonelli Lagrangian on a compact manifold, establishing new connections between weak KAM theory and the regularity of critical subsolutions of the Hamilton–Jacobi equation. The quotient Aubry set, obtained from the projected Aubry set by identifying points at zero Mañé distance, encodes essential dynamical information about the underlying Lagrangian flow. We provide a comprehensive analysis of its metric and topological properties, showing that under suitable conditions the quotient set possesses a stratified structure amenable to geometric measure-theoretic techniques.

Our principal results characterize the differentiability of critical subsolutions along the Aubry set and quantify the extent to which such subsolutions fail to be unique. We prove that critical subsolutions are constrained to coincide, up to additive constants, precisely on the classes of the quotient Aubry set, thereby recovering and refining the classical uniqueness results of Fathi and Mather. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Hausdorff dimension of the quotient Aubry set imposes sharp obstructions to the existence of $C^{1,1}$ critical subsolutions, and we construct explicit examples exhibiting quotient sets of positive dimension.

A central contribution is the development of a variational framework linking the totally disconnected structure of the quotient Aubry set—conjectured by Mather in low dimensions—to the density of smooth critical subsolutions in the sense of Bernard. We establish partial results toward Mather's conjecture, proving total disconnectedness under explicit curvature and regularity hypotheses on the Lagrangian. Our methods combine techniques from optimal transport, nonsmooth analysis, and the theory of calibrated curves, and we indicate several applications to the long-time behavior of solutions to the evolutionary Hamilton–Jacobi equation and to problems in Aubry–Mather theory for symplectic twist maps.

---

*Keywords:* weak KAM theory, Aubry–Mather theory, Hamilton–Jacobi equation, viscosity solutions, Tonelli Lagrangians, quotient Aubry set, critical subsolutions
